sections.heading: Why raw time falls short
sections.content: Shani says time is easy to measure but not a sufficient success metric: developers can write bad code quickly, so speed by itself does not show that AI improved the work.

sections.heading: What to consider instead
sections.content: There is no single metric for every AI use case. Consider a combination of code quality and security, productivity and collaboration, time gained, and developer happiness. For security tools, relevant measures include secrets prevented from leaking and issues found and fixed before shipping. Shani also suggests measuring time to value: how long from assigning a task until its value is realized, which companies may define through revenue, adoption, or time to market. The broader question is whether AI improves developer productivity, efficiency, and happiness while contributing to business value.

sections.heading: Why time alone falls short
sections.content: Shani says there is no single right metric for AI tools. A developer may finish faster but produce poor code, so elapsed time by itself does not show success. Companies need to translate time saved into outcomes such as efficiency and productivity, while considering developer happiness as well.

sections.heading: What to measure instead
sections.content: Use a combination of measures suited to the tool and task. These can include code quality and security—for example, secrets prevented from leaking and issues detected and fixed before shipping—as well as productivity, collaboration, and time gained. Shani also suggests measuring time to value: how long from assigning a developer a task until the work delivers its full value, which a company might define through revenue, adoption, or time to market. The broader goal is to assess whether AI makes developers more productive, efficient, and happy, and whether that contributes to business value.

answer.summary: Raw speed can reward producing poor code quickly. Shani recommends a combination of outcome-focused measures: code quality and security, productivity and efficiency, developer happiness, and business time-to-value.

sections.heading: Why raw time is insufficient
sections.content: Shani says time alone is not a quantifiable success metric: developers can write bad code very quickly. She also cautions that there is no single metric that captures AI’s impact across software development; the right measure depends on what the tool is intended to improve.

sections.heading: What to consider instead
sections.content: Use a combination of measures, such as code quality and security—for security work, for example, secrets prevented from leaking and issues detected and fixed before shipping—alongside productivity, efficiency, collaboration, and time gained. Shani says these inputs can contribute to developer happiness. For a business-facing measure, consider time-to-value: how long from assigning a task until its full value is realized, which a company might define in terms of revenue, adoption, or time to market.
